front: Why can Radix Sort beat the Ω(n log n) comparison-sort lower bound?
back: Because it never compares two elements directly — it distributes by digit value instead, so the comparison-based lower bound simply doesn't apply.

front: Radix Sort general complexity, and when does it become O(n)?
back: O(d·(n+D)) in general. If both D (digit alphabet size) and d (number of digits) are treated as constants, it becomes O(n).

front: Which digit does Radix Sort process first: most or least significant?
back: Least significant digit first (LSD radix sort).

front: Why must each digit-pass of Radix Sort be a stable sort?
back: Because an unstable pass would undo the correct ordering established by previous (less significant digit) passes.

front: For n b-bit numbers grouped into r-bit digits, what's the total Radix Sort runtime formula, and what determines the optimal r?
back: O((b/r)*(n+2^r)). If b <= log(n), optimal r=b (one digit). If b > log(n), optimal r=log(n) -- beyond that the 2^r bucket-count term dominates; below it the b/r pass-count term dominates.
No -- it requires O(n+D) extra memory for the buckets, unlike in-place comparison sorts. This is part of why it isn't ALWAYS faster than QuickSort in practice despite better asymptotics.
